title: Chlamydia Treatment, NGU and Lymphogranuloma Venereum
summary: Learn where C. trachomatis fits among causes of nongonococcal urethritis, how LGV (serovars L1–L3) presents, why a routine NAAT cannot tell LGV from other strains, and the CDC 2021 regimens: doxycycline 7 days for chlamydia and 21 days for LGV.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 62 Hit 8 (LGV, serovars L1–L3, 3-week doxycycline), Hit 10 (C. trachomatis in NGU; asymptomatic infection), Trap 4 (erythromycin not first-line) and Trap 5 (extragenital NAATs do not distinguish LGV), checked against the CDC 2021 STI treatment guidelines (Workowski 2021, full text via Europe PMC) and the FDA 2019 press release on extragenital NAAT clearance. Corrections: Trap 4 presents azithromycin and doxycycline as equal first-line options; CDC 2021 makes doxycycline the recommended regimen (existing register flag rv-ct-regimen). Hit 8 omits proctocolitis, the most common LGV presentation (proposed flag rv-ch62-lgv-proctocolitis). Not verified and not taught: the “groove sign” and “painless” ulcer wording, the 30–50% NGU share and 85–90% asymptomatic figure for men (CDC gives fewer than half and says asymptomatic infection is common), and the statement that no LGV-specific NAAT is FDA cleared. US regulatory and treatment content; Philippine rules are not covered.

objectives: Place C. trachomatis among the causes of nongonococcal urethritis.
Describe the main presentations of LGV and explain why a routine NAAT cannot identify it.
State the CDC 2021 recommended and alternative regimens for chlamydia and the regimen for LGV.

scenes.title: Same bug, same course?
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: two clinic patients. (1) A man with urethral discharge; Gram stain shows inflammation but no intracellular diplococci; first-void urine NAAT is positive for C. trachomatis. (2) A man with bloody rectal discharge and tenesmus; rectal swab NAAT is positive for C. trachomatis. Question token: “Same bug: same drug, same number of days?”

cues.text: Two men, one positive result. The first has urethral discharge, no gonococci on the smear, and a urine NAAT positive for Chlamydia trachomatis.
The second has bloody rectal discharge and painful straining. His rectal swab NAAT is also positive for Chlamydia trachomatis.
Same organism on the report. Do they get the same drug, for the same number of days?

props.label: Same drug, same number of days?

scenes.title: Two kinds of chlamydia infection
scenes.altText: Schematic: two strain groups. Serovars A–K: mild or asymptomatic infection, and asymptomatic infection is common; C. trachomatis is a well-established cause of nongonococcal urethritis (NGU) but accounts for fewer than half of NGU cases overall, varying by population. Card: other NGU causes in CDC 2021 — M. genitalium about 10–25%, T. vaginalis 1–8%, no pathogen found in about half even with extensive testing. Serovars L1–L3 cause lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV): severe inflammation and invasive infection.

cues.text: Chlamydia trachomatis comes in two broad groups. Serovars A through K cause mild or symptom-free infection. Symptom-free infection is common in both men and women.
In men, these strains are a well-established cause of nongonococcal urethritis. But they explain fewer than half of cases overall, and the share varies by population.
Mycoplasma genitalium causes about ten to twenty-five percent, Trichomonas one to eight percent, and in about half of cases no pathogen is found even with extensive testing.
Serovars L1, L2 and L3 are different: they cause lymphogranuloma venereum, a severe, invasive infection.

scenes.title: What LGV looks like, and what NAAT can see
scenes.altText: LGV card (CDC 2021): rectal exposure → proctocolitis, the most common presentation, mimicking inflammatory bowel disease (mucoid or bloody discharge, anal pain, tenesmus, fever); untreated, chronic fistulas and strictures; rectal LGV can be asymptomatic. Heterosexual presentation: tender, typically unilateral inguinal or femoral lymphadenopathy with possible buboes; a self-limited ulcer or papule at the inoculation site, often gone by presentation. Lab card: a routine C. trachomatis NAAT detects both LGV and non-LGV strains but does not tell them apart; definitive diagnosis needs LGV-specific molecular testing (PCR genotyping), not widely available. In 2019 the FDA cleared the first two NAATs for throat and rectal specimens (Aptima Combo 2, Xpert CT/NG).

cues.text: Rectal exposure can cause proctocolitis, the most common presentation of LGV. It can mimic inflammatory bowel disease, and if untreated it can leave fistulas and strictures. Rectal LGV can also be silent.

Among heterosexuals, a common picture is tender, usually one-sided swelling of the groin lymph nodes, sometimes with pus-filled buboes. A small ulcer or papule may appear first, but it is often gone by the time the patient seeks care.
In the lab, a routine chlamydia NAAT detects LGV and non-LGV strains, but it cannot tell them apart. A definitive LGV diagnosis needs LGV-specific molecular genotyping, which is not widely available.
In 2019 the FDA cleared the first two NAATs for throat and rectal specimens. They detect chlamydia at those sites; they do not type it as LGV.

scenes.title: The regimens
scenes.altText: Treatment table (CDC 2021, nonpregnant adults). Chlamydia: recommended doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days; alternatives azithromycin 1 g single dose or levofloxacin 500 mg daily for 7 days; erythromycin no longer recommended (gastrointestinal side effects → nonadherence). Azithromycin had more microbiologic failures in men and lower efficacy for rectal infection (one trial in MSM: cure 100% doxycycline vs 74% azithromycin). LGV: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days. Hook answers: (1) doxycycline 7 days; (2) proctocolitis with rectal NAAT positive → presumptive LGV treatment, doxycycline 21 days.

cues.text: For ordinary chlamydia, the 2021 CDC guideline recommends doxycycline, one hundred milligrams twice daily for seven days. Azithromycin one gram once, or levofloxacin, are alternatives.

Why demote azithromycin? It had more microbiologic failures in men and works less well on rectal infection. In one trial of rectal chlamydia, cure was one hundred percent with doxycycline and seventy-four with azithromycin.
Erythromycin is no longer recommended: its frequent stomach side effects can lead patients to stop taking it.

LGV gets the same drug for longer: doxycycline twice daily for twenty-one days. So patient one takes seven days. Patient two, with proctocolitis and a positive rectal NAAT, is treated presumptively for LGV, twenty-one days.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Azithromycin 1 g and doxycycline are equal first-line choices” (✓ CDC 2021: doxycycline recommended, azithromycin an alternative); “Erythromycin is a first-line option” (✓ no longer recommended because of gastrointestinal side effects); “A positive rectal NAAT tells you whether it is LGV” (✓ routine NAATs detect both but cannot tell them apart; LGV-specific genotyping is needed).

cues.text: Trap one: azithromycin and doxycycline are equal first-line choices. Not since 2021: doxycycline is recommended, and azithromycin is the alternative.
Trap two: erythromycin is a first-line option. No: it is no longer recommended because of stomach side effects.
Trap three: a positive rectal NAAT tells you whether it is LGV. No: routine NAATs detect both kinds but cannot tell them apart.

props.title: ✗ “Rectal NAAT + tells you it is LGV.”

scenes.title: Seven for ordinary, twenty-one for L
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Doxy is the default: SEVEN days for the ordinary strains, THREE weeks for the L strains — L for Lymph, L for Long.” Tokens: A–K = 7 days · L1–L3 = 21 days · NAAT sees both. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: doxycycline is the default. Seven days for the ordinary strains, three weeks for the L strains: L for lymph, L for long. And the routine NAAT sees both.
Where it breaks: LGV most often shows up in the rectum, not the groin; CDC treats symptom-free LGV with a seven-day course; pregnancy changes the drug choices; and these are United States regimens.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Chlamydia: doxycycline 7 days · azithromycin = alternative · no erythromycin”, “LGV (L1–L3): routine NAAT cannot tell it apart → doxycycline 21 days”.

cues.text: Treat ordinary chlamydia with seven days of doxycycline, keep azithromycin as the alternative and erythromycin off the list, and remember that a routine NAAT cannot tell lymphogranuloma venereum from other strains, so suspected lymphogranuloma venereum gets twenty-one days.

props.label: Chlamydia: doxy 7 d · azithro = alternative · no erythromycin
LGV L1–L3: NAAT can’t tell it apart → doxy 21 d

explanation.what: Plain language: most chlamydia strains cause mild infection that is often silent; a few strains (L1–L3) invade and cause lymphogranuloma venereum. The usual lab test finds chlamydia but cannot say which kind. Doxycycline for a week treats ordinary chlamydia; LGV needs three weeks. Scientific terms: serovars A–K, serovars L1–L3, lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), proctocolitis, buboes, nongonococcal urethritis (NGU), nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), extragenital (rectal, oropharyngeal) specimens, LGV genotyping.
explanation.why: LGV is invasive and needs a longer course; ordinary chlamydia is often asymptomatic and spreads unnoticed. Because the routine NAAT does not type the strain, the clinical picture (especially proctocolitis) decides when to treat for LGV. Azithromycin was demoted to an alternative because it had more microbiologic failures in men and lower efficacy for rectal infection.
explanation.measure: CDC 2021: chlamydia — doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days; alternatives azithromycin 1 g once or levofloxacin 500 mg daily for 7 days; erythromycin no longer recommended. LGV — doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days. NGU — C. trachomatis under half of cases overall; M. genitalium about 10–25%; T. vaginalis 1–8%; no pathogen in about half.
explanation.differs: Serovars A–K (mild or asymptomatic, 7-day doxycycline) vs L1–L3 (invasive, 21-day doxycycline); routine CT NAAT (detects both) vs LGV-specific genotyping (distinguishes, not widely available); recommended (doxycycline) vs alternative (azithromycin, levofloxacin) vs no longer recommended (erythromycin).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: choose the recommended regimen for uncomplicated chlamydia, the duration for LGV, recognise that erythromycin is not first-line, or identify that a positive rectal NAAT does not establish LGV.

questions.stem: Under the CDC 2021 STI treatment guidelines, what is the recommended regimen for uncomplicated urogenital chlamydia in a nonpregnant adult?

options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Correct. This is the recommended regimen in the 2021 guideline.

options.text: Azithromycin 1 g orally as the preferred single dose
options.rationale: Incorrect. Azithromycin 1 g is an alternative, used for example when adherence to doxycycline is a substantial concern.
Incorrect. Erythromycin is no longer recommended because gastrointestinal side effects lead to nonadherence.

options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 21 days
options.rationale: Incorrect. The 21-day course is the LGV regimen, not the regimen for uncomplicated chlamydia.

questions.stem: A man has proctocolitis with bloody rectal discharge and tenesmus. A routine rectal C. trachomatis NAAT is positive. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The routine NAAT detects LGV and non-LGV strains but cannot tell them apart; LGV-specific genotyping is needed for a definitive diagnosis
options.rationale: Correct. CDC 2021 says NAAT detects both LGV and non-LGV strains and that a definitive LGV diagnosis needs LGV-specific molecular testing, which is not widely available; a positive rectal NAAT with severe proctocolitis is treated empirically for LGV.

options.text: A positive routine NAAT rules out LGV
options.rationale: Incorrect. The routine NAAT also detects LGV strains.

options.text: Complement fixation serology should be used routinely to confirm LGV
options.rationale: Incorrect. CDC 2021 says chlamydia serology should not be used routinely to diagnose LGV.

options.text: Treatment should wait for culture confirmation
options.rationale: Incorrect. CDC 2021 says persons with a clinical syndrome consistent with LGV, such as proctocolitis, should be treated presumptively, without waiting for confirmation.

questions.stem: A man has urethritis, and his urethral smear shows inflammation without diplococci. Which statement about the causes of nongonococcal urethritis is supported by CDC 2021?

options.text: C. trachomatis is a well-established cause but accounts for fewer than half of cases overall
options.rationale: Correct. The guideline says prevalence varies across populations and is under 50% overall.

options.text: C. trachomatis accounts for more than 90% of cases
options.rationale: Incorrect. It accounts for fewer than half of cases overall.

options.text: With extensive testing, a pathogen is found in nearly every case
options.rationale: Incorrect. No pathogen is identified in about half of cases even with extensive testing.

options.text: Trichomonas vaginalis is the most common cause
options.rationale: Incorrect. T. vaginalis accounts for about 1–8% of cases, depending on population and location.

claims.text: Serovars A–K cause mild or asymptomatic infection; L1–L3 cause LGV, a severe invasive infection; asymptomatic infection is common in men and women.
C. trachomatis is a well-established NGU cause but under 50% of cases overall; M. genitalium about 10–25%; T. vaginalis 1–8%; no pathogen in about half.
LGV presentations: proctocolitis most common, mimics IBD, fistulas/strictures; unilateral tender inguinal/femoral nodes, buboes; self-limited ulcer often gone; rectal LGV can be asymptomatic.
Routine NAAT detects LGV and non-LGV strains but does not distinguish them; definitive diagnosis needs LGV-specific genotyping, not widely available; serology not routine; presumptive treatment.
In 2019 the FDA cleared the first two NAATs (Aptima Combo 2, Xpert CT/NG) for throat and rectal specimens.

Chlamydia: doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days recommended; azithromycin 1 g or levofloxacin alternatives; erythromycin no longer recommended (GI side effects); rectal trial 100% vs 74%. LGV: doxycycline 21 days; asymptomatic LGV 7 days.
Reviewer Hit 8 “painless ulcer” and “groove sign” wording.
claims.note: Not found in the sources read; not taught.

claims.text: Reviewer Hit 10: C. trachomatis causes 30–50% of NGU; 85–90% of infected men are asymptomatic.
claims.note: CDC 2021 gives under 50% overall (varies by population), which does not contradict the 30–50% range but does not confirm it, and says asymptomatic infection is common without a percentage; not taught.

claims.text: Reviewer Trap 5: LGV-specific NAATs exist but none are FDA cleared; there are exactly two FDA-cleared extragenital NAATs.
claims.note: FDA 2019 confirms the first two extragenital clearances. CDC 2021 (proctitis section) says molecular testing for LGV is not widely available or not FDA cleared, which is consistent with the reviewer as of 2021; current clearance status of LGV-specific or later extragenital assays was not checked; not taught.

claims.text: Scenario invented; strain and test visuals schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 62 Trap 4 presents azithromycin 1 g single dose and doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days as equal first-line options. CDC 2021 recommends doxycycline; azithromycin 1 g is an alternative (with levofloxacin). The lesson teaches the 2021 hierarchy (register flag rv-ct-regimen).

Ch. 62 Hit 8 describes LGV only as painless ulcer → suppurative buboes (“groove sign”) → fibrosis/strictures. CDC 2021 states proctocolitis after rectal exposure is the most common LGV presentation, the ulcer is self-limited and often gone at presentation, and rectal LGV can be asymptomatic; “groove sign” and “painless” were not found in the sources read and are not taught (proposed register flag rv-ch62-lgv-proctocolitis).

Ch. 62 Hit 10 gives C. trachomatis as 30–50% of NGU and 85–90% of infected men as asymptomatic. CDC 2021 gives fewer than half of NGU overall, varying by population, and says asymptomatic infection is common without a figure; the lesson teaches the CDC wording (proposed register flag rv-ch62-ngu-ct-share).

Ch. 62 Trap 5 (FDA clearance of extragenital NAATs, none for LGV-specific NAATs) and the treatment regimens are US-specific (FDA, CDC). The FDA 2019 release confirms the first two extragenital clearances, and CDC 2021 says LGV molecular testing is not widely available or not FDA cleared; current clearance of LGV-specific or later assays was not checked; Philippine regulatory status and treatment guidance are not covered (proposed register flag rv-ch62-extragenital-naat-us).
